entries.title: An Unsettling Glimpse Into the GOP’s Future
entries.summary: James Fishback lost badly in Florida but showed that there’s support for bigotry among the young.
entries.content:
James Fishback lost badly in Florida but showed that there’s support for bigotry among the young.

Normally, when a primary candidate finishes with 10.5 percent of the vote, it is a clear signal of their irrelevance.

James Fishback finished third in Tuesday’s Florida Republican gubernatorial primary, and at no point in the race did it seem like he ever had a chance. In fact, at no point in his broader career has the 31-year-old, who is known for his racist slurs and unabashed bigotry, achieved anything of note. The high-school-debate nonprofit he founded was hit with allegations that he had sexually groomed a 17-year-old employee. A hedge fund where he’d once worked said that it had planned on firing him before he resigned, and accused him of claiming a job title that had never existed at the firm. He founded his own investment firm but left after the board decided to shut down the funds he managed. Fishback told me that he had left the firm to run for governor. He claims to have been an adviser to DOGE—but former senior DOGE officials have denied it.

However, Fishback is defiantly proud of his showing, despite losing the primary to Representative Byron Donalds and also finishing well behind Lieutenant Governor Jay Collins. “I would much rather have gotten 10 percent and done all of this and really moved the needle in political discourse,” he told me today, “than have gotten 24 percent like Jay Collins did and have nothing to show for it.”

Despite his penchant for spectacular, serial failure, Fishback matters because he managed to figure out at least one thing: how to capture attention from the youthful right. Heading into Election Night, this was the one area where Fishback appeared to excel. A February poll from the University of North Florida found Fishback to be the leading candidate among GOP primary voters under 35, with 31 percent supporting him. By July, that number was up to 51 percent, according to a Change Research poll paid for by the conservative nonprofit Freedom Project USA. His candidacy was, in some respects, a test run for what might work with the next generation of Republican voters. What seems to be working is unrepentant bigotry.

Fishback’s appeal to younger voters can be explained by a few other things: He is relatively young. He ran a rage-bait campaign that met young people where they are, maintaining a heavy digital presence with posts and appearances on the livestreams of prominent influencers. He spoke with sympathy of the economic concerns of downwardly mobile youth. He did all of this while regularly tossing off casual racism and anti-Semitism.

During the campaign, he referred to Byron Donalds, who is Black, as By’rone and called him a “slave” to donor and corporate interests. When a Black man questioned Fishback about the grooming allegations against him, the Florida politician said that the man should be “lynched.” When I reached out to him earlier today, he doubled down: “I think anyone should be executed” for making those kinds of “false allegations,” he said. When I pressed him on why he’d specifically said “lynched” instead of “executed,” he trailed off before claiming that he might have actually gained votes for saying this. He has made not-so-subtle overtures to Groypers—slang for fans of the white-supremacist internet personality Nick Fuentes—by reportedly claiming that he rebuffed a PAC that offered him $500,000 under the condition that he rebuke Fuentes. “I hung up the phone, because I will never disavow patriotic Americans,” he told a crowd. He has used the term goyslop, anti-Semitic internet slang suggesting that there’s a Jewish conspiracy to harm the Gentile masses by feeding them junk food.

Fishback contests the “anti-Semitic” label. “I’ve condemned anti-Semitism repeatedly. It has no place in our society. Neither does the hatred of Christians,” he said when I questioned him about his use of goyslop and his praise of Groypers as “insightful” and “patriotic.” Fishback also pushed back against most of the ways he’s been described in the media. He said that he has “never claimed to be a DOGE adviser” even though he posted on X last year that he has “advised DOGE.” Fishback has maintained that the sexual-misconduct allegations are “completely false,” and he reiterated this to me, saying that no court ever found him guilty.

If you’re not prone to anti-Semitism and don’t enjoy far-right politics, it’s tempting to see Fishback as an aberration. When poll-tracking websites observed that Fishback seemed to be dominating campus precincts in Florida on Tuesday, several pundits were quick to point out that, in many cases, winning meant accruing only dozens of votes, because few students had returned to campuses from summer break. “FSU has 46,184 students. Twenty-eight people voted in this precinct. Fishback got 25,” wrote the conservative communications strategist Erica Knight. “He didn’t capture the youth vote. He captured a group chat.”

But the signs of a shift to the hard right among young Republican voters have been well documented. The New York Young Republicans Club’s Nazi tendencies are well known. A Yale poll from this past spring found that younger voters are more anti-Semitic than older generations.  And a Manhattan Institute poll from December found that 25 percent of Republicans under the age of 50 openly express anti-Semitic views. “I do see the youth right turning the dial up on misogyny, anti-Semitism, and racism—even as the youth right is racially and ethnically diverse,” Lauren Lassabe Shepherd, a historian who has written about American campus conservatism, told me when I asked her about Fishback. She suspects that the “online populism and anti-establishment politics” that Fishback espouses are here to stay.

In my own coverage of the right, I’ve observed a steady uptick in the far-right drift of young conservatives. At large right-wing events, young conservatives have consistently espoused a deeply nativist strain of politics, and expressed their fandom of Fuentes and his politics. Even young right-wingers who don’t like Fuentes have told me that they’ve witnessed the growing influence of his politics or that they agree with his views and simply see him as an imperfect vessel. Young Republican staffers on Capitol Hill are increasingly open to his far-right, Groyper style of politics.

Fishback was able to show that the energy Fuentes and other young far-right figures online have tapped into isn’t just an internet or a conservative-staffer phenomenon. It’s an ideology that someone savvier and more skilled than Fishback might well leverage to achieve greater real-world success at some point in the near future.

entries.title: Why Is Everyone in Silicon Valley Talking Like That?
entries.summary: Did you mix something up? Maybe you’re just “hallucinating.”
entries.content:
Did you mix something up? Maybe you’re just “hallucinating.”

Silicon Valley has long had its own dialect. Venture capitalists are always talking about the value of being “high agency” and making “orthogonal bets.” But lately, tech vernacular has taken a peculiar turn—people have started describing themselves as if they were chatbots. If you misspeak, maybe you’re “hallucinating.” Don’t know the answer to a question? That’s because it’s not in your “training data.” Feeling forgetful? Perhaps you have a case of “context rot,” a phrase that refers to the degradation of a bot’s responses over a long conversation. “I’ve been telling my wife I have context rot for months,” Conor Bronsdon, the host of an AI-focused podcast, told me.

Where I live, in San Francisco, such comparisons are inescapable. “I’ve described myself as high temperature,” a friend recently told me; in AI-speak, this means he is prone to randomness. AI experts now talk about updating their “weights” when they learn something new and training on “synthetic data” when going over internal thoughts. “Humans have a huge base model trained over billions of years of evolution,” one software engineer wrote on a popular tech forum. “It’s impressive how quickly we learn, but it’s arguably comparable to fine tuning.”

Such speech easily comes off as unsettling, if not aggressively bleak: Why describe beautiful, tender life in detached, algorithmic terms? At the same time, language is a fossil record of previous technological revolutions, and if this current transformation is anything like previous ones, some of this new slang may well stick around. AI experts have repeatedly cautioned that anthropomorphism, or the tendency to attribute human qualities to nonhuman objects such as chatbots, can be misleading. But now the reverse is occurring in everyday speech—a sort of modelmorphism, wherein people describe themselves as if they were large language models.

The comparisons really took off a few years ago, after a group of AI researchers argued that language models are “stochastic parrots” that link together language based on statistical patterns without possessing any understanding of meaning. Dissenters retorted that humans are also “stochastic parrots.” As one software engineer riffed, “Humans are basically a sophisticated Markov chain. They are very good at pattern matching, but have no understanding of anything.”

Language has historically evolved alongside technology. Expressions such as running out of steam and cog in the machine, for instance, were adopted into common speech after the Industrial Revolution as shorthand for the human condition. AI metaphors are simply figures of speech, Anna Ivanova, a cognitive scientist at Georgia Tech, told me: When someone says, “My gears are turning,” they don’t literally mean that there are gears or gearlike things in their brain that are actually moving; in much the same way, when people say that they have “context rot,” they don’t mean that they literally have a transformer-based AI model running in their brain.

The difference between earlier technologies and AI systems is that artificial neural networks are loosely inspired by the brain itself. Philosophers such as Raphaël Millière and Cameron Buckner have argued that LLMs could serve as potential models of certain aspects of human cognition. In the 2010s, scientists found parallels between how image-recognition neural networks and the human brain process visual information. There may also be “parallels” between how LLMs and humans represent language, Ivanova said. The MIT neuroscientist Ev Fedorenko and others have identified a type of “language network” inside the human brain, which Fedorenko believes is “very similar in many ways to early LLMs.” These comparisons are contested, but they are receiving research attention: “The recent success of LLMs is rooted in the same computational principles that govern biological brains,” scientists wrote in a position paper last week.

“Because we do not understand the brain very well we are constantly tempted to use the latest technology as a model for trying to understand it,” the philosopher John Searle wrote in the 1980s. “I am told that some of the ancient Greeks thought the brain functions like a catapult.” In the 19th and 20th centuries, people turned to telegraphs and telephone switchboards as models for the mind: “The brain is no more than a kind of central telephonic exchange,” the philosopher Henri Bergson once wrote. By the ’60s, some scholars were arguing that the mind functions like a computer. “Cognitive scientists often say that the mind is the software of the brain,” the philosopher Ned Block explained in 1990. Today, LLMs make for an alluring comparison.

For now, these analogies are being made mostly by those working in the AI industry. But over time, some of the metaphors might start to seep into everyday language. If you look at the growth of railroads, “a whole range of language change began to happen” as people started to use the new transportation system, Naomi Baron, a linguist and professor emerita at American University, told me. Some of the AI slang isn’t introducing new phrases into English so much as transforming the meaning of existing speech. Take the word hallucinating, which is used to describe AI models confabulating. People are “taking a term created for what the human mind is capable of doing, projecting it onto AI, and then projecting it back onto humans with an AI flavoring,” Baron explained.

None of this is to say every AI-inflected term should get a free pass. I’ve started chastising my friends when I catch them unironically referring to themselves as chatbots. Using LLM metaphors to describe our minds could lead to a reductive and dehumanizing understanding of human cognition. Earlier this year, when OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was pressed on AI’s natural-resource demands, he said that “it also takes a lot of energy to train a human.”

Still, the people in tech I spoke with told me that using LLM-speak to describe their own mind helps them reflect on their cognitive habits. Language subsumes new idioms over time and masks their origins. People today say “My plans have been derailed” without much thought to the phrase’s railroad origins. Perhaps my great-grandchildren will grow up saying things such as “I have context rot” and “That’s not in my training data” without pausing to remember that those phrases first applied to machines.

entries.title: President Trump Has a Pet-Project Docket at the National Parks
entries.summary: The National Park Service changed the way it prioritizes projects so that the president’s requests are quickly approved.
entries.content:
The National Park Service changed the way it prioritizes projects so that the president’s requests are quickly approved.

President Trump gets what he wants, when he wants it, from the National Park Service. One and a half million dollars to replace brick pavers in Lafayette Park, across from the White House? Contracting officials at the NPS Washington headquarters found the money within five days last month. A $170,000 request to remove a fence around the Hains Point golf course, preparing the ground for a new “championship-quality” layout? Six days this summer. And the more–than–$5 million project to gild equine statues along the nearby Memorial Bridge? That took 12 days.

The rapid-approval system is specific to projects Trump wants, thanks to a reorganization at the Interior Department led by Secretary Doug Burgum. Trump issued an executive order to make the District of Columbia “safe and beautiful,” justifying the creation of an NPS docket of “White House priorities” that is handled separately from other park projects and is prioritized both for funding and contracting resources, according to documents I obtained and interviews with five current or former NPS officials. Meanwhile, many other projects throughout the nationwide system of parks are languishing.

The list I received includes Trump’s well-known projects on the National Mall and the refurbishment of the White House, along with several lesser-known efforts: The hiring and equipping of 450 new U.S. Park Police officers in the Washington region, and more than $12.8 million—some of which came from the Department of Justice—for police equipment, including new Flock license-plate-reading cameras, radios, tasers, laptops, body cameras, and body armor. Internal documentation for park projects typically includes “Consequences of Failure to Act,” which scores the urgency based on health and safety measures. When work began in January on fountains near the White House, officials described the need for the work in this way: “Such failure will disappoint visitors, as well as residents and employees of the White House.”

The new project-funding system was described by a contracting officer during an April meeting with NPS officials. “There’s three different lists: White House priorities, high priorities, and low priorities,” the official told colleagues on the virtual call, according to a written account that was provided to me. Those on the call, who do not work on White House priorities, were advised that projects on the low-priority list likely would not be completed, so they should attempt to get their needs moved to the high-priority list. White House priorities, meanwhile, were nonnegotiable. As Washington is beautified at great expense, officials told me, vital needs at dozens of national parks are not being filled.

I obtained copies of the high- and low-priority lists that circulated this summer inside the NPS. As of mid-July, that low-priority list included 1,573 projects, including many that officials told me would have been funded under prior administrations. Projects that have not yet been funded from that list, according to a separate national-park database, include requests for new wildlife-resistant dumpsters in Bryce Canyon National Park, snow machines to provide fire remediation in Alaska’s remote Yukon–Charley Rivers National Preserve, and an archaeological survey of recently acquired land at Camp Nelson National Monument, a major Union supply base during the Civil War that trained Black soldiers.

The Interior Department dismissed the concerns over this approach when I reached out for comment and told me that the low-priority list I had obtained included items that had been “mis-prioritized and were corrected.” Interior leaders have also boasted about new funding streams, including revenue from more expensive national-park passes for foreign visitors. “In any year, the National Park Service must prioritize projects most in need,” the press office said in an unsigned statement. “The National Park Service has not only been focused on beautifying the district for the 250th celebrations in our nation’s capital but has also been working on many deferred maintenance projects throughout the country.”

But those working in the parks say that it is not just money holding these projects back. It’s also a lack of staff, after rounds of workforce reductions, who are able to handle contracts, a problem that the contracting official on the April call referred to as “capacity.” When Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency targeted the department last year, many contracting managers at the NPS took buyouts, and many of those who remained found themselves reassigned within the larger department. The NPS had 179 full-time administrative officers in June, a 21 percent decrease from the month Trump took office, according to Office of Management and Budget records. The result is a growing backlog of unfinished projects in far-flung parks, as government employees try to jury-rig temporary fixes, the officials said. “There is very little acquisition support,” one of the NPS employees told me. “This is going to get exponentially worse.”

Spencer Morgan, the site superintendent of the Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site, in Buffalo, New York, told me that his facility is still waiting on this fiscal year’s promised operating-support funding, which needs to arrive before the end of September, or he will have to institute major cuts. He has been told that an additional stream of routine-maintenance funding he was expecting will never arrive. Because the site is run in conjunction with a local nonprofit that pays Morgan’s salary, he said that he was comfortable speaking openly about the struggles his staff faces as funding and resources are instead directed to the White House list. “I am not beholden to hold my tongue at this point,” he said.

Inside the NPS, Morgan said, the staff has been decimated. “I started in this role in April of 2024, and the number of people who are not there since I started is gut-wrenching,” he told me. “There is a whole loss of institutional knowledge.”

Other NPS employees requested anonymity to speak with me because they fear retaliation from their supervisors. One employee told me that their park can’t hire employees to fill vacant slots but also can’t contract out work, because it’s difficult to get on the high-priority list. “We keep being told to be creative,” this employee said. “And we are running into dead ends every time we try to pivot.”

This reduction in spending showed up in budgetary documents I reported on in June. The documents showed a decrease of $854 million, or 68 percent, in spending on projects in park regions outside the Washington area in the first eight and a half months of fiscal year 2026, compared with the full prior fiscal year. During that same period, spending around Washington increased by about $100 million, not counting about $310 million in donations that the NPS received from allies of the president, most of which is going to fund a new White House ballroom.

The frustration over these shifting priorities has been a frequent topic of conversation among park superintendents, who are struggling to maintain services this summer. At another NPS meeting in early July, an employee presented a list of 133 projects, totaling $35.8 million, that they said were ready to go but lacked contracting staff to make them happen, according to a person on the call.

It’s not clear whether all of the projects on the White House priority list will receive funding this fiscal year. The list also includes a $25 million plan to replace the Eagle One helicopter used by the U.S. Park Police (and at least once by Burgum when he was running late for an Air Force One flight), $475,000 to clean and repaint the White House exterior, drones “to support law enforcement” in the Washington region, a new park-police substation for Rock Creek Park, and streetlight replacement along the National Mall. The priority list also includes improvements for parts of the country where Trump is known to travel. The document shows a $77,300 expense to clear brush and plant new trees around Camp David, the presidential retreat in Maryland, as part of a much larger effort to plant 3,000 trees and provide a “security benefit” to the facility.



And Trump continues to add more projects to the list—or expand projects already on it. Take, for example, the brick pavers in Lafayette Park outside the White House gates. In May, Trump said that the park renovation would be funded by “a contribution that I made,” even though internal documentation shows public funds being used. After the Fourth of July celebrations, the NPS agreed to pay an additional $1.5 million to replace more of the brick pavers in that park. Then, in August, the president told reporters in the Oval Office that he was still deliberating on whether the brick pavers were good enough.

“Now we have a big decision to make,” he said. “Do we take the pavers that are red—you know, the red-brick pavers—and do we change them into a granite, to gray granite? They’re beautiful, but they’re not the original. So we’re gonna have to make that decision.” The National Park Service, no doubt, will be ready to follow the president’s lead if he pivots.

entries.title: Another Pot of Paint Thrown in the Public’s Face
entries.summary: Does AI actually belong in an art museum?
entries.content:
For several months, something discomfiting has been creeping onto San Francisco’s lampposts, bulletin boards, and restaurant windows: more and more signs, for run clubs and a July 4 parade and tacos, all of which are obviously entirely produced by generative AI.

This bothers me terribly. (Friends have called it a fixation.) But why does it bother me? A ChatGPT-generated poster for a garage sale seems legitimately dispiriting compared with a handwritten flyer, or even a haphazardly formatted Word document. What about a bodega using an AI-generated image of a hamburger instead of a random piece of clip art pulled from the internet? It’s not like most of these flyers were ever going to be high art anyway. Still, the issue nags at me constantly, whenever I pass one of these synthetic images plastered over the real world.

Last month, in part looking for a reprieve from the AI onslaught, I went to what promised to be an imaginative new exhibition of Henri Matisse and other fauvists’ work at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. The show was centered on Femme au chapeau (“Woman With a Hat”), a foundational painting in modern art. Matisse depicted his wife with colors that were totally detached from reality: teal patches of skin, an orange-and-green neck, a phantasmagoric hat. In 1905, when the painting debuted, this was scandalous: “A pot of paint has just been thrown in the public’s face,” one critic declared.

Walking through the galleries, I was taken aback by what struck me as a scandal of its own. The museum, in collaboration with Google Arts & Culture, had used generative AI to augment visitors’ experience—in ways I found, at least initially, rather off-putting.

Part of the exhibition’s conceit was to re-create Femme au chapeau’s historical context. The museum commissioned a local artist to develop wallpaper that could have been in the palace where the painting debuted and worked with an animator to create a visual projection of the walls of Gertrude and Leo Stein’s living room, where the canvas hung for many years. I loved all of that. But an AI-generated animation of the streets of Paris circa 1905, with shadowy figures walking to the gallery and a dirigible floating above, felt more like a gimmick than historical immersion. The museumgoers around me, however, seemed awed.

Then, near the gallery’s exit, came the second AI experiment: a row of screens, each showing an expanded Matisse painting made with Veo, Google’s video-generation model. A painting of a seashore became a 3-D rendering in fauvist style; a portrait of a girl with green eyes was reimagined to place the girl in Matisse’s studio.

The fauvists painted the world with flat slabs of highly saturated hues, delighting in color for the sake of color rather than realism. Using AI to move beyond the frame and give the images “realistic” depth seemed antithetical to their original vision. I recalled childhood memories of being entranced by various Matisse works at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City, marveling at his Dance and The Piano Lesson. The AI videos alienated me rather than inviting me in.

Yet maybe I’m just a grump? I am at least open to the possibility that my response is not so different from that of the pot-of-paint conservatives in the early 1900s. So I reached out to the museum’s chief curator, Janet Bishop, to learn more about these AI experiments—how they’d been conceived, what effect they had on the show, and what role AI broadly has to play in traditional art museums. We met at the galleries, where Bishop told me that curators wanted to “give a sense of what early-20th-century Parisians or visitors to the Grand Palais would have experienced in approaching this imposing exhibition hall and then going into the sprawling 1905 salon.” The AI installations resulted from extensive human research and oversight. I came away, to my surprise, not unconvinced of these experiments’ utility—though still a bit skeptical of their tastefulness.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Matteo Wong: How did your collaboration with Google Arts & Culture come about?

Janet Bishop: It was early in 2026. We were fairly far along in terms of planning for the exhibition. We had secured all the artwork by that point and were in the process of developing a couple of the ideas that we had for how to situate visitors, such as by re-creating the gallery where Matisse’s painting made its debut at the 1905 Salon d’Automne in Paris and the successive scandal.

Our original idea for the opening gallery, where we wanted to bring our visitors back in time to turn-of-the-century Paris, was to project a lantern slide that is an image of the Grand Palais. Then our museum director, Christopher Bedford, and head of education and community engagement, Gamynne Guillotte, got back from a really inspiring trip to the Google Arts & Culture offices in London and proposed the idea of setting still images in motion.

Through our curatorial research, we had postcards, still images, interior shots, exterior shots, and other material to work with. So in what became weekly meetings with Google Arts & Culture and project team members, we reviewed the images we had and developed this film.

Wong: What does having the animated film provide to a visitor that projecting the lantern slide and displaying postcards wouldn’t?

Bishop: We have some archival displays throughout the exhibition. But what we’re programming for in this entrance gallery is to give people a sense of what it felt like to approach the Salon d’Automne in a more immersive way.

Wong: Someone could look at this AI animation and its imperfections and perhaps find it kitsch. Were you worried about that at all?

Bishop: “AI-generated” makes it sound like AI did it by itself or that this was quick and easy. The project was very labor-intensive, and everything is historically accurate. One moment that was especially exciting to me was when we were looking at a draft, and there were all of these figures that were moving away from the building, and I said to the Google engineer, “Oh my gosh, it would be so amazing if we could have them walk toward the building,” and she said, “No problem.”

Wong: Is it harder now to get people to come here and engage with the art, especially younger folks? Or is this something that would have been just as helpful decades ago?

Bishop: You were talking about your experience as a child going to MoMA, and now we recognize that people have a lot of things that command their attention. One of the challenges in getting people to art museums is just pulling people away from their screens.

People are used to experiencing content in a really wide variety of ways. I know that it is important to our director that, given our proximity to Silicon Valley, we pay attention to developing technology and how it might enhance visitor experience. I loved the idea of the original lantern slide as a projection, but I can say that I think this film does something different in terms of giving our visitors a sense of the energy of Paris around the turn of the last century.

Wong: I’d also like to talk about the other AI collaboration with Google in the exhibition, near the exit. Can you tell me the origins of this one?

Bishop: The thought for what we called the “Experiment” was to enter into the world of a select number of Matisse paintings and imagine the context for those paintings beyond what is represented on the canvas. For instance, with The Girl With Green Eyes, we don’t know who the sitter was, but we do know that it was made in Matisse’s studio. So in the Experiment, you see the figure get up and walk across the studio. The details of the studio are consistent with his actual studio, which—we know what it looks like. And she looks out the window across the Seine.

Wong: Clearly a lot of visitors are enjoying this, but I wanted to ask why you thought it was important to help people imagine the world beyond the frame. My initial reaction, if I’m being honest, was that there’s a frame for a reason, and that the paintings aren’t naturalistic for a reason. What was so shocking 100 years ago was that these were, like, just flat planes of color, and that the colors were the focus. To turn that into a three-dimensional seascape seems almost wrong or off-putting.

Bishop: It’s part of our interest in engaging with different sorts of learners, people of different ages. They’ve been very popular with kids, and these images of paintings might encourage people to look more closely at the actual paintings. We’re experimenting, and I think experimentation is very definitely what we embraced with these features within the exhibition.

Wong: You mentioned earlier that you were excited by changing the historical AI video to have visitors walking toward the palace, rather than away from it. Was there a similar moment of excitement here?

Bishop: The big surprises came for me in the first piece, where in terms of the ability to conjure an experience, the use of AI as a tool made us more effective in achieving our goals than would have been possible without it. So that was really actually quite exciting. I think the Experiment is a little bit less integral to the story but an engaging feature that I’m happy that we pursued.

entries.title: The ‘Resistance’ Won
entries.summary: The much-derided movement was right about Trump’s nature, and how to defeat him.
entries.content:
The much-derided movement was right about Trump’s nature, and how to defeat him.

Donald Trump celebrated the defeat of one of his first impeachment nemeses—retired Army Lieutenant Colonel Alex Vindman, who lost the Democratic Senate primary in Florida on Tuesday—in typical form. “SleazeBag Vindman loses tonight to a Radical Left Lunatic. How cool is that???” Trump exulted on Truth Social.

Vindman served as a witness in Trump’s first impeachment. Whatever currency this once gave him with Democratic voters has long since expired. In this, he is not unique. Democrats such as Dan Goldman, George Conway, and Tom Steyer, all of whom pushed for or played prominent roles in Trump’s first impeachment, have discovered in primaries this year that this credential means little to their party’s voters. Diana DeGette, a House manager during Trump’s second impeachment trial, and Harry Dunn, a Capitol Police officer who battled insurrectionists, have also lost primaries.

The rout of the Democratic Party’s impeachment stars has been interpreted, generally, as a sign of the end of resistance politics. “The string of losses for resistance candidates from the first Trump term illustrates a new era for the restive Democratic base, where vocal opposition to the president through official channels and public remonstrations no longer guarantees success,” Politico reports.

The “resistance,” once a dominant mode of Democratic politics during the first Trump administration, was never cool. But in the second term, the “resistance liberal” has fallen out of favor so completely that the phrase has become a derisive punch line across the political spectrum. Which is a shame, because the resistance was, broadly speaking, correct. It was right about Trump’s nature, and also right about how to defeat him.

Resistance politics depicted Trump as a crook and an aspiring authoritarian with a troubling fondness for dictators, especially Vladimir Putin. He was a con man, unfit for office, and had broken faith with the best traditions of American politics. The Robert Mueller investigation found, among other things, that Putin had dangled a lucrative no-risk deal to Trump during the 2016 campaign. The Senate Intelligence Committee, found, in a bipartisan report, that the campaign’s links to Russia posed a “grave counterintelligence threat.” The first impeachment charged Trump with having “placed his own personal and political interests above the national interests of the United States, sought to undermine the integrity of the U.S. presidential election process, and endangered U.S. national security.”

These much-derided processes turned out to supply an accurate, almost banal, description of how Trump has operated during his second term. His corruption and abuses of power have been let loose at a scale that was previously only imagined. Trump has all but severed America’s system of alliances, mocked and bullied Ukraine’s president, and showered praise upon Kim Jong Un.

What discredited resistance politics in liberal eyes is that it was closely associated with institutional procedures that were deemed to have ultimately failed to restrain Trump. Mueller’s investigation ended anticlimactically. Neither impeachment drew enough Republican support to remove Trump from office. Somewhat similarly, conservatives have sometimes claimed that the Russia investigation and first impeachment helped Trump politically by drawing to his side Republicans who resented the overreach.

One Republican who doesn’t seem to believe either of these arguments is Trump. The president has worked hard to ensure that no such humiliations recur during his second term, by stacking the Justice Department with loyalists, firing inspectors general en masse, purging the armed forces of “woke” officers, and generally eliminating any potential source of independence within the federal government.

Trump himself does not seem to think that the investigations that were avidly followed by resistance liberals did nothing to restrain his actions during his first term, or that they helped him shore up partisan support. And the absence of any such processes in his second term has not made Republicans in Congress feel freer to criticize the president. To the contrary, their fealty is more absolute than ever.

Even in the first term, resistance Democrats were dogged by their populist left-wing critics. This split first appeared in the spring of 2017, when Jon Ossoff ran to fill a special election for a House seat in Georgia, in a previously Republican district. Ossoff’s campaign, which attacked Trump’s corruption but declined to articulate a sharp progressive alternative, fell short.

Supporters of Bernie Sanders blamed Ossoff, and the party, for not taking up the Sanders message. “Ossoff’s campaign has failed to support or address any progressive issues. He embraces a centrist—not progressive—message, that both political parties waste taxpayer money, rather than politicians being corrupt by outside money,” the progressive writer Michael Sainato complained in the Observer. Winnie Wong, a co-founder of People for Bernie, told The Guardian of Ossoff, “He didn’t have a core progressive message and that ultimately is why he lost.” (Ossoff won a Senate race in 2020 and is leading the polls again this year, making slashing attacks on Trump’s personal corruption while steering clear of controversial left-wing policy stances.)

Like the Republican critics of resistance politics, progressive ones depicted it as substituting legal tactics for electoral victories. Yet the resistance was never limited to cheering on Mueller or hoping to persuade Republicans to convict the president of high crimes and misdemeanors. Resistance themes inspired the Democrats’ political message during Trump’s first term. And that message landed. Democrats retook the House in the 2018 midterms, despite a hot economy, and then defeated Trump’s reelection effort. Joe Biden, a link to a bygone era of civility and bipartisanship, ran in 2020 on a message of restoring the soul of America. He won.

Once in office, however, Biden ceded his domestic agenda to progressives who believed in Sanders’s vision of transformational change. They believed that only overturning the neoliberal order, handing control of domestic policy to neo-Brandeisians and climate hawks, and giving unions almost every policy they demanded would allow Democrats to regain the trust of working-class voters. This theory, not the resistance, failed. Biden’s support collapsed within his first year, and Kamala Harris’s half-hearted efforts to distance herself from her unpopular boss were too little, too late.

Trump’s return to office has left Democrats casting about for a stronger and more effective response. Perhaps the most obvious solution is the one they hit upon when Trump was first elected nearly a decade ago: Rather than promise to change everything about American politics, focus relentlessly on Trump’s unfitness. The crisis in the United States is not the general corruption of both parties; it is the specific corruption of Trump and his enablers. And the solution is simply to replace the corrupt, racist authoritarian with a governing party that respects the rule of law, equality, and basic decency.
